sections.title: Elements of Probability: Sample Spaces and Events

slides.title: A measurement of maybe
slides.kicker: Like length and area, but for chance
bullets: Probability is a type of measurement, just like length, area or volume — but it measures the likelihood of events.
It expresses how confident or certain we are that a particular event will occur.
The book asks: Will it rain today? Will our school win the hockey match? Will I be picked in the lucky draw?
slides.note: Chance ko bhi measure karte hain — meter ki tarah!

slides.title: Random events around you
bullets: A random event has known possible outcomes, but no sure result in advance — chance is involved every time.
Rain or no rain; the hockey match can end in a win, draw or loss; exactly one student wins the assembly lucky draw.
For the lucky draw, the names of all students are written on slips and one slip is randomly selected.

slides.title: The language of likelihood
slides.kicker: Impossible to certain, with everything between
bullets: We respond to random events with words like impossible, certain, less likely, more likely or equally likely.
Such judgments are based on different kinds of evidence that have been gathered.
Can we predict random outcomes with 100% certainty? Usually we can only weigh the possibilities.

slides.title: Subjective probability
slides.kicker: Two friends, one sky, two guesses
bullets: One friend says the sun is shining brightly, so it is unlikely to rain today.
Another friend feels the very hot air and thinks it could rain later.
Both predict rainfall by interpreting the present weather conditions — this is subjective probability.
slides.note: Chapter goal: move from guesswork to objective measurement.

slides.title: Two objective routes
bullets: Way 1: use evidence from experience — repeat an experiment or analyse past data. Relative frequency gives experimental probability.
Way 2: assume all outcomes are equally likely and reason about favourable outcomes over total outcomes. This is theoretical probability.
Theoretical methods apply when there is no reason to believe any one outcome is more likely than another.

slides.title: Outcomes and sample space
slides.kicker: Every result an experiment can give
bullets: In an experiment, the event that results is called an outcome.
The set of all possible outcomes in an experiment is called the sample space, listed in brackets separated by commas.
A tossed coin gives the sample space {H, T}; a rolled 6-sided die gives {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

slides.title: Experimental probability formula
bullets: Experimental Probability equals the number of times the event occurred divided by the total number of trials.
Repeat the experiment many times, count how often the event happens, then divide.
Relative frequency shows probability from actual data rather than theoretical predictions.

items: Divide by total number of trials

slides.title: Fifty rolls, sixteen percent
bullets: Roll a die 50 times and it lands on 4 exactly 8 times.
The experimental probability of rolling a 4 is 8/50 = 0.16, which is 16%.
The relative frequency of rolling a 4 is also 8/50 = 0.16 — especially useful in statistics and data analysis.
slides.note: Snakes and Ladders grew from ancient India's dice game Jnan-Chaupad!

slides.title: Rules of a sample space
slides.kicker: Complete list, no repeats, size n(S)
bullets: The sample space S is the list of all possible outcomes; each outcome is an element of the sample space.
S must include every possible outcome, and no outcome should be listed more than once.
The number of elements is the sample size, written n(S).
A match gives S = {Win, Lose, Draw} with n(S) = 3; rain gives S = {Rain, No Rain} with n(S) = 2.

slides.title: Sample spaces can grow
slides.kicker: Match the detail to the question
bullets: For a plain rain-or-not question, S = {Rain, No Rain} works fine.
To include amounts of rainfall, expand to {No Rain, Drizzle, Light Rain, Heavy Rain}.
A good sample space is detailed enough to suit the specific problem being studied.

right.title: Detailed space
items: {No Rain, Drizzle, Light Rain, Heavy Rain}

slides.title: An event is a subset
slides.kicker: Pick the outcomes you care about
bullets: An event is any single possible result or combination of results that might happen in a random action.
Formally, an event is a subset of the sample space.
Two coins: the event at least one Head is E = {HH, HT, TH}, three of the four outcomes.
One die: the event greater than 4 is E = {5, 6}, two of the six outcomes.

slides.title: Why draw a tree
bullets: A tree diagram is a visual representation that lists all possible outcomes of a multi-step experiment.
A multi-step experiment is a series of independent trials, like tossing a coin two times or rolling a dice three times.
Each branch shows a possible outcome; each complete path from start to end is one full outcome.

slides.title: Building the two-coin tree
slides.kicker: One point, two levels, four paths
bullets: From a single point, draw a line to each possible outcome of the first toss: H or T.
From each of those outcomes, draw two more lines for the second toss.
The finished tree shows 4 possible outcomes, so S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}.

slides.title: Probabilities on branches
bullets: Theoretical Probability P equals the number of favourable outcomes over the number of possible outcomes.
Write each outcome's theoretical probability on the branch representing that outcome.
Getting Heads twice is the single outcome HH, so P(HH) = 1/4 = 0.25 or 25%.
Think and Reflect: one head and one tail is {HT, TH}, so the probability is 2/4 = 1/2.
slides.note: HT aur TH dono alag paths hain — yaad rakho!

quiz.q: Probability is a measurement, most like which of these?
options: Measuring the volume of a water tank
Measuring how likely an event is
Measuring the length of a pencil
Measuring the area of a field
quiz.why: Probability measures the likelihood of events, the way length, area and volume measure physical quantities.

options: impossible, certain, less likely, more likely, equally likely

options: Estimating from experiments and estimating by theoretical reasoning
quiz.why: Experimental probability uses evidence and relative frequency; theoretical uses equally likely reasoning.

quiz.why: S must include every possible outcome exactly once: the match can end in a win, a loss or a draw.

quiz.why: E collects every outcome containing at least one H: HH, HT and TH.

options: Predict the exact result of an experiment
List all possible outcomes of a multi-step experiment

quiz.why: Only HH out of the four paths {HH, HT, TH, TT} is favourable: P = 1/4 = 0.25 or 25%.

options: Tails is the more likely single outcome
HT and TH are two separate paths, giving 2 out of 4
The coin remembers the first toss

examples.title: Fifty rolls of a die
examples.problem: Suppose you roll a die 50 times and it lands on 4 exactly 8 times. Find the experimental probability of rolling a 4.
steps: Identify the total number of trials: the die was rolled 50 times.
Count the event: the die landed on 4 exactly 8 times.
Apply the formula: Experimental Probability = number of times the event occurred / total number of trials = 8/50.
Convert: 8/50 = 0.16, which is 16%. This value is also called the relative frequency of rolling a 4.
examples.answer: Experimental probability of rolling a 4 is 8/50 = 0.16, or 16%.

examples.title: Two coin tosses on a tree
examples.problem: Toss a fair coin two times. Build the tree diagram, list the sample space, and find P(HH) and the probability of getting one head and one tail.
steps: From a single point, draw a line to each possible outcome of the first toss: H or T.
From each of these outcomes, draw two lines for the second toss; the tree shows 4 possible paths.
Read the sample space from the paths: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, so there are 4 possible outcomes.
P(HH): one favourable outcome over 4 possible outcomes = 1/4 = 0.25 or 25%.
One head and one tail: the paths HT and TH, so 2 favourable of 4, P = 2/4 = 1/2 or 50%.
examples.answer: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}; P(HH) = 1/4 = 25% and P(one head, one tail) = 2/4 = 1/2 = 50%.

examples.title: Two fruit baskets
examples.problem: Basket A has one apple and two oranges. Basket B has one banana and one mango. You randomly pick one fruit from each basket. Draw the tree diagram, list the sample space, and find the probability of picking one apple and one banana.
steps: Treat each fruit as a distinct outcome: basket A gives Apple, Orange-1, Orange-2; basket B gives Banana or Mango.
Draw the tree: 3 branches from basket A, each splitting into 2 branches for basket B — 3 x 2 = 6 equally likely pairs.
Sample space: {Apple-Banana, Apple-Mango, Orange1-Banana, Orange1-Mango, Orange2-Banana, Orange2-Mango}, so n(S) = 6.
The event 'one apple and one banana' contains only the pair Apple-Banana, so there is 1 favourable outcome.
examples.answer: The sample space has 6 pairs; the probability of picking one apple and one banana is 1/6.

examples.title: Pens with replacement
examples.problem: A box contains 3 red pens, 4 black pens and 2 green pens. You pick a pen without looking and put it back, then your friend does the same. Find the probability that you both pick pens of the same colour.
steps: Total pens = 3 + 4 + 2 = 9. Because each pen goes back, both picks have the same 9 possibilities.
Ordered pairs of distinct pens: 9 x 9 = 81 equally likely outcomes.
Same-colour pairs: red-red gives 3 x 3 = 9; black-black gives 4 x 4 = 16; green-green gives 2 x 2 = 4.
P(same colour) = favourable / possible = 29/81, which is about 0.36.
examples.answer: P(both pens the same colour) = 29/81, approximately 0.36 or 36%.
